name: Dana Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Anything you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a six-person firm in the town I grew up in, run by Mr Brennan, who's sixty-six. Our clients are dairy farmers, the builders' merchant, a funeral home and the parish, people I've known since I was little. I do their year-end accounts and tax returns, and half the farmers still bring in their invoices in a biscuit tin.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people trust me with their business, and that I can walk down the high street and know who I've helped. The hard part is the deadlines, and the new software the government keeps making us file through. I don't use any of the AI programs, I check everything by hand and I sleep better for it.

S0.quote: I'm not scared of a computer taking my job, I'm scared of my boss Mr Brennan retiring and selling us to a firm that's never met a farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's what I've thought all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a fad, like a lot of things from the big cities. At church or with Tomás's family I'd say good, people still need someone they can trust. I don't go online much, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI isn't what worries me. Mr Brennan is sixty-six with no children in the business, and he's hinted a bigger firm from the city wants to buy us. I'm not scared of a computer taking my job, I'm scared of my boss Mr Brennan retiring and selling us to a firm that's never met a farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, the same clients, the same way. Tomás and I would keep putting money into the wedding fund for next June. I'd maybe ask Mr Brennan straight out what his plans are, which I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but with that worry about the firm in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you have set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two months of bills, plus the wedding fund, which we won't touch. Tomás earns less than me at his family's garage, so my pay matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm was sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to stay on, because the farmers would want me. But a city firm might want everything done on their own systems, and I'd struggle with that.

say: I'd call AI a **big-city fad** that came to nothing.
I'd say people still need **someone they trust** with their books.
think: My real worry is **Mr Brennan retiring** and selling the firm.
A **city buyer** might not value farmers or my way of working.
do: Carry on doing **year-end accounts** for the same local clients.
Keep saving into the **wedding fund** for next June.
Ask Mr Brennan directly about his **retirement plans**.
feel: **Steady**, with a **background worry** about the firm's future.
fieldNote: Dana's worry predates AI: a **possible sale** of a small family firm.
Her pay is the **bigger income** in the household, which raises the stakes.
She **distrusts** city firms and new systems more than the technology itself.

steps.text: Keep doing year-end accounts for the dairy farmers and parish
Keep paying into the wedding fund for next June

S1.quote: My clients' trust is worth something, but not if a program does the same return for half the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking. That's what I do all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it in public the way my dad would: hard work and knowing your clients still count. With Tomás's family I'd say the farmers won't trust a computer. I'd stay off the internet about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Mr Brennan would jump at software that does the returns, or a buyer would. The farmers would grumble but they'd pay less, and they'd take it. My clients' trust is worth something, but not if a program does the same return for half the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, but I'd start saving harder, maybe another hundred and fifty a month, and cut down on takeaways and the new car Tomás wanted. I'd have to learn whatever software the firm forced on us, but I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd also ask Father Michael if he knows any parish or charity roles that need a bookkeeper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's tilting under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say clients won't trust a computer, but you also think they'd take the cheaper fee. Which do you really believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second one, if I'm honest. People say they want the personal touch, but they look at the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your fiancé about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we wait. Tomás can keep the old van running another two years, he's a mechanic after all.

say: I'd say **hard work** and knowing your clients still count.
I'd tell family the farmers **won't trust a computer**.
think: Mr Brennan or a buyer would happily use software for **the returns**.
Clients would grumble but accept **half the fee**.
do: Save another **£150 a month** and cut takeaways.
Put off the **new car** Tomás wanted for two years.
Ask **Father Michael** about bookkeeping roles at parish charities.
feel: Like the **ground is tilting** beneath her.
fieldNote: She admits the **gap** between her public faith in trust and private realism.
Her support network is **church and family**, not courses or forums.
She would learn new software only if **forced**.

steps.text: Save an extra £150 a month from her pay
Postpone the new car and keep Tomás's old van running
Ask Father Michael about bookkeeping work at parish charities
Keep doing returns at Mr Brennan's firm as normal

S2.quote: Giving up the hotel for the wedding would hurt, but a parish hall wedding with a job afterwards beats a hotel wedding with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? We'd barely be married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's God's world and we'll get through it like families always have. At church I'd say look after each other. I wouldn't blame the farmers, I'd blame the tech companies who rushed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd lose my job, probably within a year of it arriving. Everything I do is at a desk with numbers, and the machine does that better. Tomás's garage is hands-on, so he'd have about three years more than me, and then robots come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the wedding smaller, the parish hall instead of the hotel, and put the difference into savings. I'd ask Tomás's dad if I could do the garage's books and run the front desk. We'd probably move into the flat above the garage to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd pray about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the smaller wedding mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Giving up the hotel for the wedding would hurt, but a parish hall wedding with a job afterwards beats a hotel wedding with nothing. My mum would be upset, she's been planning it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the garage's books really pay you a wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a full one. Maybe half of what I earn now. We'd get by on that and Tomás's pay for a while, but not forever.

say: I'd say families will **get through it** like they always have.
I'd **blame the tech companies** for rushing it.
think: I'd **lose my job** within a year of AGI arriving.
Tomás's garage has about **three more years** before robots.
do: Hold a **parish hall** wedding instead of the hotel and save the difference.
Do the garage's **books and front desk** for Tomás's dad.
Move into the **flat above** the garage to save rent.
fieldNote: Dana expects **job loss** and a fall to about **half pay**.
The **wedding** is the first thing she'd cut, which hurts her family.
Her plan rests entirely on **Tomás's family garage** and its robot gap.

steps.text: Hold the wedding at the parish hall instead of the hotel
Do the books and front desk at Tomás's family garage
Move into the flat above the garage
Lean on Tomás's pay and family while income halves

S3.quote: Learning the AI just to keep a desk job for two more years feels like polishing the shoes I'm about to throw away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit of breathing room, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years to look after our own. At church I'd say the young ones should learn a trade. I still wouldn't post anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose my job around 2030 or 2031, maybe sooner if Mr Brennan sells. Five years gives us time to get married properly and maybe buy something small. But the end is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hotel wedding but cut the guest list. I'd save hard, aiming for six months of bills by 2029. And I'd start learning the garage side, the parts ordering and customer bookings, so I can step in when my job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less panicked. Like I can see the cliff from further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any AI tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Learning the AI just to keep a desk job for two more years feels like polishing the shoes I'm about to throw away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait. I'd want to know there's a steady income before a baby. That's the hardest part to say out loud.

say: I'd say we have **a few years** to look after our own.
I'd tell young people at church to **learn a trade**.
think: I'd **lose my job** around 2030 or 2031, sooner if the firm sells.
Five years lets us **marry properly**, but the end is the same.
do: Keep the hotel wedding but **cut the guest list**.
Save towards **six months** of bills by 2029.
Learn the garage's **parts ordering** and bookings to step in later.
feel: **Worried**, but able to see the cliff from **further off**.
fieldNote: She still **expects** to lose her accounting income within five years.
Refuses AI tools as **wasted effort** on a dying job.
Delaying **children** is the cost she finds hardest to say.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list but keep the hotel
Save towards six months of bills by 2029
Learn parts ordering and bookings at Tomás's garage
Wait on having a baby until income is steady

S4.quote: If the firm's sold, I'd rather work for my husband's family than for strangers in an office I've never seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people work hard and plan. I'd tell people at church not to panic. I'd say the government should leave it to families and businesses to sort out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep my job for most of the decade, especially if Mr Brennan doesn't sell. By 2036 I'd want to be part of the garage business properly, maybe a partner. Tomás and I could have a child in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the firm and save steadily. I'd wait a few years to see whether the AI really arrives as fast as people say, because I've heard these predictions before. Around 2032 I'd move over to the garage full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Brennan sold to a city firm, I'd move to the garage straight away. If the firm's sold, I'd rather work for my husband's family than for strangers in an office I've never seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the garage be safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever, maybe until 2039. But by then we'd have the business and the building, and that's something.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** for people who plan.
I'd say **families and businesses**, not government, should sort it out.
think: I'd likely **keep my job** for most of the decade.
By 2036 I'd want to be a **partner** in the garage.
do: Carry on at the firm and **save steadily** each month.
**Wait** a few years to see if AGI really arrives.
Move to the **garage full time** around 2032.
fieldNote: She still expects her **accounting income** to end, just later.
Her **traditional outlook** shows in leaning on family over government.
A **sale** of the firm is her trigger to leave early.

steps.text: Keep doing accounts at Mr Brennan's firm
Save steadily from each month's pay
Wait a few years before believing the AGI forecasts
Move to Tomás's family garage full time around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd be newly married with my job gone and only the garage. What would help is if firms had to give people proper notice and help them into local trades, and if small family businesses got tax breaks to keep people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what clients lose. When a farmer's wife rings me crying about a tax bill, she wants someone from her own town to say it'll be all right.

headlineQuote: When a farmer's wife rings me crying about a tax bill, she wants someone from her own town to say it'll be all right.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old accountant** at a six-person family firm in her home town.
Her clients are **farmers, the parish** and local businesses she's known all her life.
She's engaged to Tomás, a **mechanic** at his family's garage, and never uses AI.
Her first worry is her **boss selling** the firm, before any AI.
In every AGI picture she falls back on **the garage**, cutting wedding and baby plans.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, newly married with her job gone and only **the garage**.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **notice** and help into local trades, plus **tax breaks** for family firms.
